idiom_name: start-up acquisition phase: one init hook, owned and validated resources
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give the process (or the owning object) one explicit initialisation phase that runs before the resource is needed, acquire and validate everything the critical path will use, and keep the result in an owner that releases it deterministically. Sequence consumers so none can run before the phase completes (blocking bootstrap, readiness gate or dependency-ordered construction) and make the phase idempotent so it can be replayed after a reload or a deploy. Where the runtime already guarantees eager initialisation - package initializers, static/type initializers, module load, pre-main static construction - that mechanism replaces the hand-written bootstrap; the classic structure is still justified where the runtime is lazy by default (class loading, lazy bindings), where acquisition is fallible and the failure must be reported rather than cached, or where the acquisition must also be re-runnable. Decide the failure policy first: an acquisition failure is either fatal (refuse to start), degradable (continue without the resource, or with a stub) or retried under a bounded budget.
code_sketch:
init_phase():                        # runs once, before the first deadline
    pool = provider.open_pool(min_idle=N)    # acquire
    pool.validate()                          # prove it works
    owner.adopt(pool, release=pool.close)    # own it, with a release rule
ready.signal()                       # consumers/readiness may proceed
pitfalls: Letting consumers run before the acquisition phase completes reintroduces the cold path - now with two code paths to reason about.
Acquiring eagerly but never releasing, or releasing in a different scope than the one that acquired, leaks the resource for the process lifetime.
A non-idempotent phase double-opens pools, double-registers listeners or leaks the previous instance when it is replayed.

Wrong move: eager-acquiring every bean or component 'just in case' (Spring's eager-singleton default applied without triage) -> start-up time, memory and the boot-time failure blast radius grow with the eager set while most of it serves code paths nobody calls -> instead keep the eager set to the critical path and mark optional beans lazy so only deadline-bearing resources are boot-warmed.

Wrong move: prewarming more than the target cache can hold (e.g. pg_prewarm over a whole relation larger than shared_buffers) -> the load evicts its own lower-numbered blocks and other hot pages, so the 'warmed' start is colder than a targeted one -> instead prewarm the hot working set in block ranges and measure the hit-ratio gain before widening the eager set.

Wrong move: treating a green boot as proof the eager resources work -> a pool filled without validation still fails the first checkout when credentials expired or a middlebox reaped the idle connections -> instead validate each eager resource with a canary call or ping inside the eager phase and gate readiness on that validation, not on successful construction.
